claim: The computational design of a symmetric protein homo-oligomer that binds a symmetry-matched small molecule larger than a metal ion has not yet been achieved.
source: The computational design of a symmetric protein homo-oligomer that binds a symmetry-matched small molecule larger than a metal ion has not yet been achieved.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work, presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: A de novo designed homo-trimeric protein binds the C3 symmetric small molecule drug amantadine with each protein monomer making identical interactions with each face of the small molecule.
source: We used de novo protein design to create a homo-trimeric protein that binds the C3 symmetric small molecule drug amantadine with each protein monomer making identical interactions with each face of the small molecule.
evidence: This is the primary claim of the manuscript, supported by experimental data presented throughout including NMR, X-ray crystallography, and neutron diffraction.

claim: Solution NMR data show that ABP has regular three-fold symmetry.
source: Solution NMR data show that the protein has regular three-fold symmetry and undergoes localized structural changes upon ligand binding.
evidence: Supported by NMR experimental data presented in Figure 2d and described in the Results section.

claim: ABP undergoes localized structural changes upon amantadine binding.
source: Solution NMR data show that the protein has regular three-fold symmetry and undergoes localized structural changes upon ligand binding.
evidence: Supported by NMR titration data showing chemical shift changes in Figure 2d and 2e.

claim: The high-resolution X-ray structure of ABP reveals a close overall match to the design model with the exception of water molecules in the amantadine binding site not included in the Rosetta design calculations.
source: A high-resolution X-ray structure reveals a close overall match to the design model with the exception of water molecules in the amantadine binding site not included in the Rosetta design calculations, and a neutron structure provides experimental validation of the computationally designed hydrogen-bond networks.
evidence: Supported by X-ray crystallography data showing RMSD of 0.63 Å and the presence of water molecules mediating hydrogen bonds (Figure 3).

claim: A neutron structure provides experimental validation of the computationally designed hydrogen-bond networks in ABP.
source: A high-resolution X-ray structure reveals a close overall match to the design model with the exception of water molecules in the amantadine binding site not included in the Rosetta design calculations, and a neutron structure provides experimental validation of the computationally designed hydrogen-bond networks.
evidence: Supported by neutron diffraction data showing hydrogen bond networks (Figure 3e-f).

claim: There has been progress in the de novo design of small molecule binding proteins.
source: While there has been progress in the de novo design of small molecule binding proteins (Tinberg et al., 2013; Ollikainen et al., 2015; Mills et al., 2016; Polizzi et al., 2017; Dou et al., 2018), there are still considerable challenges in this area (Dou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work in the field.

claim: There are still considerable challenges in the de novo design of small molecule binding proteins.
source: While there has been progress in the de novo design of small molecule binding proteins (Tinberg et al., 2013; Ollikainen et al., 2015; Mills et al., 2016; Polizzi et al., 2017; Dou et al., 2018), there are still considerable challenges in this area (Dou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review of challenges in the field.

claim: There has been progress in designing protein structures with internal symmetry.
source: There has also been progress in designing protein structures with internal symmetry (Boyken et al., 2016; Ghirlanda et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Designing symmetric protein homo-oligomers that bind to symmetry matched small molecules enables more economical design strategies in which one protein-small molecule interface is utilized multiple times.
source: From the protein design standpoint, this challenge is interesting as it enables more economical design strategies in which one protein-small molecule interface is utilized multiple times, analogous to the use of a single designed protein-protein interface in self-assembling protein nanostructures (Bale et al., 2016; Hsia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a logical inference about design efficiency, supported by analogy to self-assembling protein nanostructures.

claim: Ligand induced homo-oligomerization systems are increasingly in demand in cellular engineering applications.
source: From the applications standpoint, the challenge has considerable importance because it provides a stepping stone to ligand induced homo-oligomerization systems, which are increasingly in demand in cellular engineering applications (Fegan et al., 2010; DeRose et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to applications in cellular engineering.

claim: Chemically-inducible dimerization systems have been utilized to modulate signal transduction.
source: Chemically-inducible dimerization systems (Spencer et al., 1996) have been utilized to modulate signal transduction (Spencer et al., 1996; Mallet et al., 2002; Guerrero et al., 2008), transcriptional activation (Nyanguile et al., 1997), and post-translational modification (Stankunas et al., 2003), and as components for logic gates (Miyamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous applications.

claim: Chemically-inducible dimerization systems have been utilized for transcriptional activation.
source: Chemically-inducible dimerization systems (Spencer et al., 1996) have been utilized to modulate signal transduction (Spencer et al., 1996; Mallet et al., 2002; Guerrero et al., 2008), transcriptional activation (Nyanguile et al., 1997), and post-translational modification (Stankunas et al., 2003), and as components for logic gates (Miyamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Chemically-inducible dimerization systems have been utilized for post-translational modification.
source: Chemically-inducible dimerization systems (Spencer et al., 1996) have been utilized to modulate signal transduction (Spencer et al., 1996; Mallet et al., 2002; Guerrero et al., 2008), transcriptional activation (Nyanguile et al., 1997), and post-translational modification (Stankunas et al., 2003), and as components for logic gates (Miyamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Chemically-inducible dimerization systems have been utilized as components for logic gates.
source: Chemically-inducible dimerization systems (Spencer et al., 1996) have been utilized to modulate signal transduction (Spencer et al., 1996; Mallet et al., 2002; Guerrero et al., 2008), transcriptional activation (Nyanguile et al., 1997), and post-translational modification (Stankunas et al., 2003), and as components for logic gates (Miyamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: No chemically-inducible trimerization systems have been developed.
source: However, to our knowledge, no chemically-inducible trimerization systems have been developed despite the importance of trimerization in pro-apoptotic and pro-inflammatory signaling cascades (Spencer et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of such systems in the literature, presented as knowledge.

claim: Trimerization is important in pro-apoptotic and pro-inflammatory signaling cascades.
source: However, to our knowledge, no chemically-inducible trimerization systems have been developed despite the importance of trimerization in pro-apoptotic and pro-inflammatory signaling cascades (Spencer et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on signaling cascades.

claim: Amantadine is an FDA approved drug.
source: We focused on the C3 symmetric compound amantadine as it is an FDA approved drug (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2009/016023s041,018101s016lbl.pdf) with a low side effect profile (Perez-Lloret and Rascol, 2018).
evidence: Supported by reference to FDA documentation.

claim: Amantadine has a low side effect profile.
source: We focused on the C3 symmetric compound amantadine as it is an FDA approved drug (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2009/016023s041,018101s016lbl.pdf) with a low side effect profile (Perez-Lloret and Rascol, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review of amantadine's safety profile.

claim: Amantadine has C3 symmetry.
source: We focused on the C3 symmetric compound amantadine as it is an FDA approved drug (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2009/016023s041,018101s016lbl.pdf) with a low side effect profile (Perez-Lloret and Rascol, 2018).
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge about the molecular structure of amantadine.

claim: ABP was designed starting from parametrically generated C3 symmetric helical bundle backbones consisting of two concentric rings each with three helices.
source: To de novo design amantadine-binding sites at the protein trimer C3 axes, we started from parametrically generated C3 symmetric helical bundle backbones consisting of two concentric rings each with three helices.
evidence: This describes the computational design methodology used.

claim: The symmetry axes of the protein scaffold and the amantadine were aligned during the design process.
source: The symmetry axes of the protein scaffold and the amantadine were aligned, and the remaining two degrees of freedom (the placement along the symmetry axis, and the rotation around this axis) were sampled by grid search (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the computational design methodology, illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The placement along the symmetry axis and the rotation around this axis were sampled by grid search during the design process.
source: The symmetry axes of the protein scaffold and the amantadine were aligned, and the remaining two degrees of freedom (the placement along the symmetry axis, and the rotation around this axis) were sampled by grid search (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the computational design methodology.

claim: RosettaDesign was used to optimize the identities and conformations of residues within 12.5 Å of amantadine for high affinity binding.
source: For each placement, RosettaDesign was used to optimize the identities and conformations of the residues within 12.5 Å of the amantadine for high affinity binding, and residue conformations at distances farther than 12.5 Å to retain hydrogen-bond networks identified by Rosetta HBNet (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This describes the computational design methodology.

claim: Rosetta HBNet was used to identify hydrogen-bond networks in residues farther than 12.5 Å from amantadine.
source: For each placement, RosettaDesign was used to optimize the identities and conformations of the residues within 12.5 Å of the amantadine for high affinity binding, and residue conformations at distances farther than 12.5 Å to retain hydrogen-bond networks identified by Rosetta HBNet (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This describes the computational design methodology, with hydrogen bond networks shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The design search was restricted to symmetric solutions in which each monomer is identical in sequence and structure.
source: The search was restricted to symmetric solutions in which each monomer is identical in sequence and structure.
evidence: This describes a constraint in the computational design methodology.

claim: A particularly low energy solution was found starting from a previously characterized design with a high-resolution crystal structure (2L6HC3_13).
source: We found a particularly low energy solution starting from a previously characterized design with a high-resolution crystal structure (2L6HC3_13) (Boyken et al., 2016) (Figure 1a and d).
evidence: This describes the computational design result, with reference to prior work and shown in Figure 1.

claim: ABP contains 19 amino acid changes compared to 2L6HC3_13.
source: This solution, which we refer to as ABP (amantadine-binding protein), contains 19 amino acid changes compared to 2L6HC3_13 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1d.

claim: The interactions critical for amantadine binding in ABP include hydrogen bonds from Ser-71 to the polar amino group of amantadine.
source: The interactions critical for amantadine binding include hydrogen bonds from Ser-71 to the polar amino group of amantadine and a shape complementary binding pocket composed by Ile-64, Leu-67, and Ala-68 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the designed binding interactions, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The interactions critical for amantadine binding in ABP include a shape complementary binding pocket composed by Ile-64, Leu-67, and Ala-68.
source: The interactions critical for amantadine binding include hydrogen bonds from Ser-71 to the polar amino group of amantadine and a shape complementary binding pocket composed by Ile-64, Leu-67, and Ala-68 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the designed binding interactions, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: ABP was expressed at high levels in the soluble fraction in E. coli.
source: The design was expressed at high levels in the soluble fraction and was found by SEC-MALS to be a trimer in the presence and absence of amantadine (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from protein expression studies.

claim: ABP was found by SEC-MALS to be a trimer in the presence and absence of amantadine.
source: The design was expressed at high levels in the soluble fraction and was found by SEC-MALS to be a trimer in the presence and absence of amantadine (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The thermofluor melting curve for apo-ABP exhibited a high initial fluorescence signal at 25°C.
source: The thermofluor melting curve for apo-ABP exhibited a high initial fluorescence signal at 25° C (Figure 2b), indicating that hydrophobic residues in the protein core are exposed to solvent, characteristic of a molten globule state.
evidence: This is supported by thermofluor assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The high initial fluorescence signal of apo-ABP indicates that hydrophobic residues in the protein core are exposed to solvent, characteristic of a molten globule state.
source: The thermofluor melting curve for apo-ABP exhibited a high initial fluorescence signal at 25° C (Figure 2b), indicating that hydrophobic residues in the protein core are exposed to solvent, characteristic of a molten globule state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the thermofluor data based on established knowledge about protein folding states.

claim: As apo-ABP was heated to 95°C, the fluorescence signal decreased, likely due to aggregation and/or complete unfolding.
source: As the protein was heated to 95° C, the fluorescence signal decreased, likely due to aggregation and/or complete unfolding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of thermofluor data with speculative reasoning about the cause.

claim: In the presence of amantadine (1 mM), the initial fluorescence signal of ABP was much lower, characteristic of properly folded proteins.
source: In the presence of amantadine (1 mM), the initial fluorescence signal was much lower, characteristic of properly folded proteins (Figure 2b), suggesting that amantadine binding may cause local ordering and exclude solvent.
evidence: This is supported by thermofluor data in Figure 2b and interpreted based on knowledge of protein folding.

claim: Amantadine binding may cause local ordering in ABP and exclude solvent.
source: In the presence of amantadine (1 mM), the initial fluorescence signal was much lower, characteristic of properly folded proteins (Figure 2b), suggesting that amantadine binding may cause local ordering and exclude solvent.
evidence: This is an inference from the thermofluor data showing reduced fluorescence upon amantadine binding.

claim: 2L6HC3_13 is thermally stable by thermofluor assay, only starting to denature at ~80°C.
source: In contrast, 2L6HC3_13, which has the same backbone parameters but lacks the amantadine binding site, is thermally stable by thermofluor assay, only starting to denature at ~80° C (Figure 2b), consistent with previous work (Boyken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by thermofluor data in Figure 2b and consistent with prior characterization.

claim: Amantadine had no effect on the melting curve of 2L6HC3_13.
source: As expected, amantadine had no effect on the melting curve of 2L6HC3_13, suggesting the interactions with ABP are through the designed binding site (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by thermofluor data in Figure 2b.

claim: The lack of effect of amantadine on 2L6HC3_13 suggests the interactions with ABP are through the designed binding site.
source: As expected, amantadine had no effect on the melting curve of 2L6HC3_13, suggesting the interactions with ABP are through the designed binding site (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is an inference from the control experiment with 2L6HC3_13.

claim: The circular dichroism spectrum of ABP at 25°C suggests an all α-helical structure, with negative bands at 222 nm and 208 nm, and a positive band at 190 nm.
source: The circular dichroism (CD) spectrum of ABP at 25° C suggests an all ɑ-helical structure, with negative bands at 222 nm and 208 nm, and a positive band at 190 nm (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: As ABP was heated to 95°C, a loss in CD signal was observed which was not significantly altered in the presence of 1 mM amantadine.
source: As the sample was heated to 95° C, a loss in CD signal was observed which was not significantly altered in the presence of 1 mM amantadine (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by CD thermal denaturation data in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ABP was selectively 13C-methyl-labeled at Ala, Ile, Leu, and Val residues in a 12C/15N/1H background for NMR characterization.
source: To examine whether the hydrophobic residues (Ile-64, Leu-67, and Ala-68) contacting amantadine (Figure 1b) undergo conformational changes upon ligand binding, as suggested by the thermofluor assays, ABP was selectively 13C-methyl-labeled at Ala, Ile, Leu, and Val residues in a 12C/15N/1H background and characterized by solution NMR, both in the presence and absence of amantadine.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for NMR studies.

claim: Resonances for 70 out of 79 amide groups and 51 out of 51 methyl groups present in the ABP primary sequence were observed by NMR.
source: We observe resonances for 70 out of 79 amide and 51 out of 51 methyl groups present in the primary sequence; a small number of amide NMR resonances are missing likely due to conformational exchange-induced line broadening.
evidence: This is an observation from NMR experiments.

claim: A small number of amide NMR resonances are missing likely due to conformational exchange-induced line broadening.
source: We observe resonances for 70 out of 79 amide and 51 out of 51 methyl groups present in the primary sequence; a small number of amide NMR resonances are missing likely due to conformational exchange-induced line broadening.
evidence: This is an interpretation of missing NMR resonances based on established NMR principles.

claim: The single set of peaks for all three polypeptide chains of apo-ABP suggests that it populates a homogeneous and symmetric ensemble of conformers in solution.
source: The single set of peaks for all three polypeptide chains of the apo-ABP suggests that it populates a homogeneous and symmetric ensemble of conformers in solution (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is an interpretation of NMR data shown in Figure 2d based on NMR principles.

claim: The 1H dispersion in the 2D 1H-15N HQMC and 2D 1H-13C HMQC NMR spectra suggests that ABP, both in the presence and absence of amantadine, adopts a similar helical structure.
source: The 1H dispersion in the 2D 1H-15N HQMC and 2D 1H-13C HMQC NMR spectra suggests that ABP, both in the presence and absence of amantadine, adopts a similar helical structure (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is an interpretation of NMR spectral features shown in Figure 2d.

claim: A full titration of amantadine on ABP confirms the formation of a stable amantadine-ABP complex.
source: A full titration of amantadine on ABP confirms the formation of a stable amantadine-ABP complex, with chemical exchange between the free and bound ABP states slow on the NMR chemical shift time scale (residence time of 10–100 milliseconds) (Figure 2d, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by NMR titration data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Chemical exchange between the free and bound ABP states is slow on the NMR chemical shift time scale with a residence time of 10–100 milliseconds.
source: A full titration of amantadine on ABP confirms the formation of a stable amantadine-ABP complex, with chemical exchange between the free and bound ABP states slow on the NMR chemical shift time scale (residence time of 10–100 milliseconds) (Figure 2d, arrows).
evidence: This is an interpretation of NMR line shapes based on NMR theory.

claim: NMR line shape fitting using TITAN suggests an apparent dissociation constant (KD) of 24.1 ± 2.7 μM for amantadine binding to ABP.
source: An NMR line shape fitting of the three most significantly affected ABP methyl resonances (>0.1 ppm chemical shift deviation between free and bound states) using TITAN suggest an apparent dissociation constant (KD) of 24.1 ± 2.7 μM and upper limit for off-rate constant (koff) of 60.7 ± 5.6 s−1 (on-rate constant of 2.5 × 106 M−1 sec−1) (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is derived from quantitative analysis of NMR titration data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: NMR line shape fitting suggests an upper limit for off-rate constant (koff) of 60.7 ± 5.6 s−1 for amantadine dissociation from ABP.
source: An NMR line shape fitting of the three most significantly affected ABP methyl resonances (>0.1 ppm chemical shift deviation between free and bound states) using TITAN suggest an apparent dissociation constant (KD) of 24.1 ± 2.7 μM and upper limit for off-rate constant (koff) of 60.7 ± 5.6 s−1 (on-rate constant of 2.5 × 106 M−1 sec−1) (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is derived from quantitative analysis of NMR titration data.

claim: The on-rate constant for amantadine binding to ABP is 2.5 × 106 M−1 sec−1.
source: An NMR line shape fitting of the three most significantly affected ABP methyl resonances (>0.1 ppm chemical shift deviation between free and bound states) using TITAN suggest an apparent dissociation constant (KD) of 24.1 ± 2.7 μM and upper limit for off-rate constant (koff) of 60.7 ± 5.6 s−1 (on-rate constant of 2.5 × 106 M−1 sec−1) (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is derived from quantitative analysis of NMR titration data.

claim: The relatively slow fitted on- and off-rate constants are consistent with a buried amantadine binding site.
source: The relatively slow fitted on- and off-rate constants are consistent with a buried amantadine binding site.
evidence: This is an inference from the kinetic data based on knowledge of binding site accessibility.

claim: Conventional fraction bound analysis yielded lower and upper bounds for the KD to be 25 μM and 55 μM, respectively.
source: We also performed an independent conventional fraction bound analysis, which yielded lower and upper bounds for the KD to be 25 μM and 55 μM, respectively (Figure 2d, inset).
evidence: This is an independent analysis of NMR titration data shown in Figure 2d inset.

claim: Amantadine likely binds to ABP with a KD in the low micromolar range.
source: Together, these data suggest that amantadine likely binds to ABP with a KD in the low micromolar range.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple NMR binding analyses.

claim: Significantly affected methyl resonances in NMR could correspond to the Ile-64, Leu-67, and Ala-68 residues in close proximity to the intended amantadine binding site.
source: We were not able to assign the resonances of the protein due to difficulties in preparing labeled samples, but we observe significantly affected methyl resonances which could correspond to the Ile-64, Leu-67, and Ala-68 residues in close proximity to the intended amantadine binding site in the designed structure (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about resonance assignments based on the design model.

claim: NMR titrations of both amide and methyl groups suggest the presence of localized backbone and side-chain conformational changes in ABP upon amantadine binding.
source: Together, the NMR titrations of both amide and methyl groups suggest the presence of localized backbone and side-chain conformational changes in ABP upon amantadine binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from NMR chemical shift perturbation data.

claim: Crystals of ABP were obtained in the presence but not the absence of amantadine.
source: Crystals were obtained in the presence but not the absence of amantadine, consistent with ordering upon amantadine binding.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from crystallization trials.

claim: The observation that crystals were obtained only in the presence of amantadine is consistent with ordering upon amantadine binding.
source: Crystals were obtained in the presence but not the absence of amantadine, consistent with ordering upon amantadine binding.
evidence: This is an inference from the crystallization results.

claim: The X-ray crystal structure of ABP+amantadine was solved to 1.04 Å.
source: The X-ray crystal structure of ABP+amantadine was solved to 1.04 Å, providing a high-resolution view of the ABP-amantadine complex structure (Figure 3a and Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: This is reported crystallographic data.

claim: The crystal structure overlays well with the design model, with an RMSD of 0.63 Å.
source: The crystal structure overlays well with the design model, with an RMSD of 0.63 Å (TMAlign [Zhang and Skolnick, 2005]) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between the crystal structure and design model shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The primary difference between the design model and crystal structure is in the compactness of helices in the amantadine-binding region and rotation of the amantadine molecule accompanied by the presence of crystallographic water molecules.
source: The primary difference between the design model and crystal structure is in the compactness of helices in the amantadine-binding region and rotation of the amantadine molecule accompanied by the presence of crystallographic water molecules (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the crystal structure to the design model, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In the original design model, the amino group of amantadine was oriented to hydrogen bond directly to Ser-71 in ABP.
source: In the original design model, the amino group of amantadine was oriented to hydrogen bond directly to Ser-71 in ABP (Figure 3b), but in the X-ray crystal structure, amantadine was found to be rotated 60° with ordered water molecules mediating hydrogen bonds to Ser-71 residues in ABP (Figure 3b–c).
evidence: This describes the designed interaction shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In the X-ray crystal structure, amantadine was found to be rotated 60° with ordered water molecules mediating hydrogen bonds to Ser-71 residues in ABP.
source: In the original design model, the amino group of amantadine was oriented to hydrogen bond directly to Ser-71 in ABP (Figure 3b), but in the X-ray crystal structure, amantadine was found to be rotated 60° with ordered water molecules mediating hydrogen bonds to Ser-71 residues in ABP (Figure 3b–c).
evidence: This is an observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 3b-c.

claim: Amantadine is often bound as a tri- or tetra-hydrate with the waters associated with the amino group.
source: Amantadine is often bound as a tri- or tetra-hydrate with the waters associated with the amino group (Thomaston et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2011), for example in a recent crystal structure of amantadine bound to the influenza M2 channel protein, amantadine bound the key His-37 residues in M2 through water-mediated interactions (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: In a crystal structure of amantadine bound to the influenza M2 channel protein, amantadine bound the key His-37 residues in M2 through water-mediated interactions.
source: Amantadine is often bound as a tri- or tetra-hydrate with the waters associated with the amino group (Thomaston et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2011), for example in a recent crystal structure of amantadine bound to the influenza M2 channel protein, amantadine bound the key His-37 residues in M2 through water-mediated interactions (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by citation and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Including explicit water molecules in the Rosetta design calculations could enable the design of proteins that bind amantadine with higher affinity.
source: Including explicit water molecules in the Rosetta design calculations could enable the design of proteins that bind amantadine with higher affinity.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future design improvements based on the observed water-mediated binding.

claim: Room temperature neutron data collected to 2.3 Å on a deuterium-exchanged ABP crystal revealed the protonation state of residues that form hydrogen bonds to the polar amino group of amantadine.
source: Room temperature neutron data collected to 2.3 Å on a deuterium-exchanged ABP crystal revealed the protonation state of residues that form hydrogen bonds to the polar amino group of amantadine and the orientation of the D2O network that helps anchor amantadine at the trimeric interface (Figure 3e–f; Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is supported by neutron diffraction data shown in Figure 3e-f.

claim: Neutron data revealed the orientation of the D2O network that helps anchor amantadine at the trimeric interface.
source: Room temperature neutron data collected to 2.3 Å on a deuterium-exchanged ABP crystal revealed the protonation state of residues that form hydrogen bonds to the polar amino group of amantadine and the orientation of the D2O network that helps anchor amantadine at the trimeric interface (Figure 3e–f; Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is supported by neutron diffraction data shown in Figure 3e-f.

claim: Nuclear scattering length density is clearly visible for the deuterium atoms of water molecules DOD-31 and DOD-41, and the amino group of amantadine.
source: Nuclear scattering length density is clearly visible for the deuterium atoms of water molecules DOD-31 and DOD-41, and the amino group of amantadine.
evidence: This is an observation from the neutron diffraction data.

claim: DOD-31 accepts hydrogen bonds from the amino hydrogens of amantadine and donates hydrogen bonds to SER-71 and DOD-41.
source: DOD-31 accepts hydrogen bonds from the amino hydrogens of amantadine and donates hydrogen bonds to SER-71 and DOD-41.
evidence: This is an observation from the neutron structure showing hydrogen bonding patterns.

claim: In both the X-ray and neutron structures, amantadine sits at a special position on the C3 symmetry axis.
source: In both the X-ray and neutron structures, amantadine sits at a special position on the C3 symmetry axis, with its adamantane moiety interlocked at the trimeric interface and surrounded by the hydrophobic residues Ile-64, Leu-67, and Ala-68.
evidence: This is an observation from both crystal structures.

claim: The adamantane moiety of amantadine is interlocked at the trimeric interface and surrounded by the hydrophobic residues Ile-64, Leu-67, and Ala-68.
source: In both the X-ray and neutron structures, amantadine sits at a special position on the C3 symmetry axis, with its adamantane moiety interlocked at the trimeric interface and surrounded by the hydrophobic residues Ile-64, Leu-67, and Ala-68.
evidence: This is an observation from both crystal structures.

claim: The neutron structure shows no evidence of H/D exchange within the trimeric interface, even though the crystals were D2O exchanged.
source: The neutron structure shows no evidence of H/D exchange within the trimeric interface, even though the crystals were D2O exchanged, suggesting that the trimeric core is tightly packed, and that once formed, remains stable and inaccessible to solvent at room temperature.
evidence: This is an observation from the neutron diffraction data.

claim: The lack of H/D exchange within the trimeric interface suggests that the trimeric core is tightly packed, and that once formed, remains stable and inaccessible to solvent at room temperature.
source: The neutron structure shows no evidence of H/D exchange within the trimeric interface, even though the crystals were D2O exchanged, suggesting that the trimeric core is tightly packed, and that once formed, remains stable and inaccessible to solvent at room temperature.
evidence: This is an inference from the neutron diffraction data about protein stability and solvent accessibility.

claim: ABP binds amantadine in a manner very similar to the design model and leads to significant localized changes as visualized by solution NMR.
source: ABP binds amantadine in a manner very similar to the design model and leads to significant localized changes as visualized by solution NMR, but it is a constitutive (albeit perhaps not a very thermal-stable) trimer in the absence of amantadine.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from NMR and crystallography.

claim: ABP is a constitutive trimer in the absence of amantadine.
source: ABP binds amantadine in a manner very similar to the design model and leads to significant localized changes as visualized by solution NMR, but it is a constitutive (albeit perhaps not a very thermal-stable) trimer in the absence of amantadine.
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data showing ABP is a trimer with or without amantadine.

claim: ABP may not be a very thermally stable trimer.
source: ABP binds amantadine in a manner very similar to the design model and leads to significant localized changes as visualized by solution NMR, but it is a constitutive (albeit perhaps not a very thermal-stable) trimer in the absence of amantadine.
evidence: This is inferred from the thermofluor data showing characteristics of a molten globule state.

claim: Sidechain truncations such as Ala/Ser mutations were introduced in the core of ABP to destabilize the trimeric interface.
source: Sidechain truncations such as Ala/Ser mutations were introduced in the core of ABP to destabilize the trimeric interface (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), but these constructs were either poorly expressed or lost amantadine binding activity as assessed by thermofluor.
evidence: This describes design attempts shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: ABP constructs with Ala/Ser mutations in the core were either poorly expressed or lost amantadine binding activity.
source: Sidechain truncations such as Ala/Ser mutations were introduced in the core of ABP to destabilize the trimeric interface (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b), but these constructs were either poorly expressed or lost amantadine binding activity as assessed by thermofluor.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from testing variant designs.

claim: The Rosetta HBNet protocol was extended to search for intermolecular hydrogen bond interactions between residues that span the monomer-monomer interfaces to reduce the extent of hydrophobic packing of the trimer.
source: The Rosetta HBNet protocol that was used to generate the hydrogen-bond networks in ABP was extended to search for intermolecular hydrogen bond interactions between residues that span the monomer-monomer interfaces reduce the extent of hydrophobic packing of the trimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), but these constructs were again poorly expressed.
evidence: This describes a computational design approach shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: ABP constructs with intermolecular hydrogen bond networks spanning monomer-monomer interfaces were poorly expressed.
source: The Rosetta HBNet protocol that was used to generate the hydrogen-bond networks in ABP was extended to search for intermolecular hydrogen bond interactions between residues that span the monomer-monomer interfaces reduce the extent of hydrophobic packing of the trimer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c), but these constructs were again poorly expressed.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from testing variant designs.

claim: Truncations of the outer helix resulted in mostly insoluble protein or monomeric species that no longer bound amantadine.
source: Truncations of the outer helix (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–f) were attempted, but this resulted in mostly insoluble protein or monomeric species that no longer bound amantadine (In one case, truncation of both helices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g) resulted in a tetramer that no longer bound amantadine).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from testing variant designs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d-f.

claim: Truncation of both helices resulted in a tetramer that no longer bound amantadine.
source: Truncations of the outer helix (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–f) were attempted, but this resulted in mostly insoluble protein or monomeric species that no longer bound amantadine (In one case, truncation of both helices (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g) resulted in a tetramer that no longer bound amantadine).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from testing a variant design shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: In larger-scale redesigns, the core amantadine-binding site was backed up with helical repeat fusions to stabilize the helical core, but these constructs remained constitutive trimers.
source: In larger-scale redesigns, the core amantadine-binding site was backed up with helical repeat fusions to stabilize the helical core (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h), but these constructs remained constitutive trimers.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from testing variant designs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: Conversion of ABP into well behaved monomers that assemble into a trimer in the presence of amantadine is difficult because the subunit-subunit interface in the trimer involves considerable non-polar surface area which makes the subunits poorly behaved as monomers.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that conversion of our design into well behaved monomers that assemble into a trimer in the presence of amantadine is difficult because the subunit-subunit interface in the trimer involves considerable non-polar surface area which makes the subunits poorly behaved as monomers, and the low binding affinity for amantadine does not provide a strong driving force for assembly.
evidence: This is an inference from the failed attempts to create an inducible trimerization system.

claim: The low binding affinity for amantadine does not provide a strong driving force for assembly.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that conversion of our design into well behaved monomers that assemble into a trimer in the presence of amantadine is difficult because the subunit-subunit interface in the trimer involves considerable non-polar surface area which makes the subunits poorly behaved as monomers, and the low binding affinity for amantadine does not provide a strong driving force for assembly.
evidence: This is an inference from the binding affinity measurements and failed assembly attempts.

claim: This is the first successful de novo design of a homo-trimeric protein that binds a C3 symmetric small molecule other than a metal ion.
source: While we were unable to design an inducible trimer, our results are an advance for protein design as to our knowledge this is the first successful de novo design of a homo-trimeric protein that binds a C3 symmetric small molecule other than a metal ion (Mills et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work, with reference to prior work on metal binding.

claim: Amantadine, given its small size, does not provide strong driving force for trimerization.
source: Our results suggest two major bottlenecks to the goal of an amantadine-inducible trimerization system based on amantadine binding at a helical bundle three-fold interface: (1) Amantadine, given its small size, does not provide strong driving force for trimerization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and binding affinity measurements.

claim: Well behaved monomers in the absence of amantadine are hard to achieve in a system with substantial buried nonpolar surface area at the trimer interface.
source: (2) Well behaved monomers in the absence of amantadine are hard to achieve in a system with substantial buried nonpolar surface area at the trimer interface (which becomes exposed in the monomers).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the failed attempts to create monomeric variants.

claim: Success in designing protein homo-trimerization systems will likely require smaller subunit interfaces and higher affinity binding sites, perhaps using larger C3 molecules.
source: Success in designing protein homo-trimerization systems will likely require smaller subunit interfaces and higher affinity binding sites, perhaps using larger C3 molecules.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future design strategies based on the lessons learned.

claim: The neutron structure of ABP has an RMSD of 0.59 Å compared to the computational model.
source: The high-resolution X-ray structure (white) and neutron structure (gray) of ABP in complex with amantadine are very close to the computational model (magenta, green, and cyan) (RMSD of 0.63 Å and 0.59 Å, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 3a.
